words.connector: Think of schema-on-read like a filing cabinet where anyone can toss in any document — there are no strict folders. The structure only matters when someone retrieves and interprets a document. Very flexible, but only if everyone who reads the cabinet agrees on what the documents mean.
words.techContext: We use MongoDB's schema-on-read for user preferences — every user can have arbitrary key-value pairs without a migration — but we added a Mongoose schema layer in the application to enforce structure and prevent malformed documents from being written.
words.exampleSentence: Schema-on-read let us onboard three new event types to the analytics pipeline in a single afternoon without any database migrations, but it also meant a missing 'timestamp' field in production data wasn't caught until the reporting query broke a week later.
words.etymology: Schema from Greek skhēma (form, figure, shape), from ekhein (to hold, to have). Read from Old English rǣdan (to interpret). The compound term was popularised in the 2010s to distinguish document and data lake approaches from traditional relational schema design.

words.shortDefinition: Storing all data for a document in one contiguous disk location so a single read fetches the full entity.
words.simpleDefinition: Document locality means that all the data you need for a single entity — say, a user profile with their address, preferences, and order history — is stored together in one place on disk. When you retrieve the document, a single disk read fetches everything. In contrast, a normalised relational schema splits that data across multiple tables, requiring multiple reads and joins.
words.longDefinition: Kleppmann explains document locality as the key performance advantage of document databases over normalised relational schemas. When an application typically accesses an entire entity at once — a user profile, a product catalogue entry, a blog post with its comments — storing all that data contiguously on disk means a single disk seek retrieves everything the application needs. In a normalised relational schema, the same data is spread across multiple tables linked by foreign keys, requiring the query planner to perform multiple index lookups, join operations, and potentially multiple disk reads to assemble the full entity. The limitation of document locality is the cost of updates: if a document is large and an update modifies only a small part of it, the entire document must be rewritten. MongoDB, for instance, stores documents as BSON and must rewrite the full document for any field change if the new value is larger than the old one (expanding the document). Document locality is therefore most valuable when documents are read frequently as a whole and written infrequently — content management systems, product catalogues, and user profiles are good fits. It is poorly suited to applications that frequently access fragments of documents or that need to join data across document types.
words.connector: Think of document locality like keeping all your medical records in a single manila folder — when the doctor asks about your history, they pull one folder, not fifteen. In contrast, a normalised database keeps your prescriptions in one cabinet, your X-rays in another, and your visit notes in a third.
words.techContext: MongoDB's document model with locality works well for our product catalogue — each product document embeds its variants, images, and metadata so a single find() call retrieves everything the product page needs without any joins.
words.exampleSentence: Document locality made the blog post endpoint 60% faster after we embedded comments directly into the post document — the API no longer needed a separate query to the comments table.
words.etymology: Document from Latin documentum (lesson, proof, example), from docere (to teach). Locality from Latin localitas (local character), from locus (place). The compound term appears in Kleppmann's framing in Chapter 2 to describe the performance trade-off specific to document data models.

words.shortDefinition: A database that natively supports multiple data models — such as documents, graphs, key-value, and relational — within a single engine and storage layer.
words.simpleDefinition: A multi-model database stores and queries data in multiple formats — documents, graphs, wide columns, key-value — through one system, eliminating the need to maintain and synchronize separate specialist databases. Applications access the data model that fits each use case while all data lives in one place.
words.longDefinition: Polyglot persistence — running multiple specialist databases for different data models — solves the impedance mismatch problem but introduces operational complexity: each database requires separate deployment, monitoring, backup, and cross-system consistency management. Multi-model databases attempt to provide the same model flexibility within a single engine. ArangoDB supports documents (JSON), graphs (edges between documents), and key-value access through a single AQL query language, with all models sharing the same underlying storage and ACID transactions. Azure Cosmos DB supports multiple APIs: document (Core SQL API), graph (Gremlin API), wide-column (Table API), and MongoDB-compatible wire protocol — all backed by a single distributed database engine, allowing developers to choose the access model without migrating data. Redis has evolved toward multi-model: it supports strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes (documents), streams, and vector indexes (with RediSearch) — a single Redis cluster can serve cache, queue, search, and vector similarity workloads. FaunaDB and SurrealDB are purpose-built multi-model databases that combine document and graph models with ACID transactions across both. Trade-offs: multi-model databases rarely match the performance of a purpose-built specialist at extreme scale; a dedicated graph database (Neo4j) outperforms a multi-model database on deep graph traversals; a dedicated time-series database outperforms on time-series compression. Multi-model databases win on operational simplicity for workloads that need multiple models at moderate scale.
words.connector: Think of a multi-model database like a Swiss Army knife — it handles documents, graphs, and key-value access in one tool, at the cost of not being the sharpest blade for any single purpose. A dedicated specialist database is the chef's knife — better for one job, but you need a separate tool for every other job.
words.techContext: ArangoDB's AQL allows a single query to traverse a graph of users and return related document data — no cross-database join required — because edges and documents share the same transactional storage layer.
words.exampleSentence: The social platform replaced its separate PostgreSQL (user profiles), Neo4j (connections), and Redis (session cache) stack with ArangoDB — a single multi-model database handled all three, reducing operational complexity significantly for their scale.
words.etymology: Multi from Latin multus ('many, much') — multiple; model from Latin modulus ('a small measure') — the data model is the structural representation of data; database from data + base, the foundational storage layer; a multi-model database supports many structural representations within one storage system.

words.shortDefinition: A group of related columns stored together in a wide-column database, enabling efficient retrieval of all columns in a family with a single row key lookup.
words.simpleDefinition: A column family is a named group of columns in a wide-column database like HBase or Cassandra. All columns in a family are stored together on disk, so reading one column in a family efficiently retrieves its siblings. Rows in wide-column databases can have different columns within a family — only columns that were explicitly written for a row are stored.
words.longDefinition: Wide-column databases (HBase, Cassandra, Bigtable) organize data differently from relational databases. Instead of a fixed schema of columns for all rows, wide-column stores use a two-level key structure: a row key identifies the row; within each row, data is grouped into column families; within each column family, individual columns can be added dynamically per row. All columns within a column family are stored together in the same storage files (HBase StoreFiles, Cassandra SSTables), making it efficient to read all columns in a family. A row can have millions of columns across families. Google Bigtable (the original wide-column store, described in the 2006 OSDI paper) stores the web crawl index with a row key of reversed domain name + URL, a column family for HTML content, and a column family for outlinks — each family is stored separately, so reading outlinks does not scan the much larger HTML content. HBase mirrors Bigtable's design. Cassandra adapts the model: partition key + clustering columns form the row key; column families are mapped to table definitions; each partition key maps to one physical row of columns stored in sorted order. Design rules for column families: keep the number of column families small (HBase recommends 1–3 per table) because each family has its own MemStore and HFile — too many families increases compaction overhead; group columns that are typically accessed together into the same family (access locality); separate infrequently accessed large columns (binary blobs) from small frequently-accessed columns into different families to avoid scanning large values on small-column reads.
words.connector: Think of a column family like the tabbed sections in a physical filing cabinet. Each drawer (row key) has dividers labeled 'Contacts', 'Invoices', and 'Contracts' (column families). Pulling all the Invoices for a client means opening one divider — you never touch the other sections.
words.techContext: HBase table design for a social network might use two column families: `cf:profile` (name, bio, avatar URL — frequently read together) and `cf:activity` (post timestamps, like counts — accessed separately); this separates storage and compaction for the two access patterns.
words.exampleSentence: By placing the high-cardinality activity log columns in a separate column family from the user profile columns, HBase's compaction ran independently on each family — profile reads became 40% faster because they no longer scanned large activity data.
words.etymology: Column from Latin columna ('pillar, column') — a vertical arrangement of values sharing a common attribute; family from Latin familia ('household') — a group of related members; column family denotes a named group of related columns that are stored and accessed together in a wide-column database.
